transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, to be perfectly honest with you, I wouldn't be here at all if it weren't for my primary care doctor. He got very... focused on my routine at my last physical. He seems quite concerned that my meal planning has gotten, in his words, "too tight." Which, frankly, I think is a bit of an overreaction. 

I mean, as an operations research analyst, my entire career is built on optimizing systems, finding efficiencies, and making sure things run predictably. So it’s only natural that I apply that same logic to my daily life. To me, it doesn't feel "tight" at all—it just feels like I'm keeping things orderly. For instance, I keep breakfast very simple, just a specific yogurt, because I know exactly what to expect and it takes zero mental energy to prepare. Then, by the time lunch rolls around, I’m usually deep into a data set or a complex model, so if I’m busy, I just skip it. It’s much more efficient than breaking my concentration, you know? It just makes sense. 

And then for dinner, I make sure it’s a very measured, precise meal. I plan it out perfectly so that the whole day just stays completely orderly and under control. It’s just a system that works for my schedule, but my doctor insisted I come speak to you about it because he doesn't seem to understand that some of us just prefer a highly structured, predictable day. I really don't see the issue with knowing exactly what goes into my body and when.
Do you ever feel anxious or upset if you're unable to stick to your planned meals?

Well, yes, I suppose I do get... a bit unsettled. Unsettled is probably the right word. Or maybe anxious, as you said. It’s just that, well, when you have a system that works perfectly, any deviation from that system introduces variables that are, frankly, very difficult to account for. 

For example, if I have to go to a restaurant—which I try to avoid because you just never know how much butter or oil they’re hiding in things—or if I just end up eating a dinner that isn't perfectly measured according to my usual specifications, I feel it immediately. And then, the next morning, if I step on the scale and it’s up even a single pound... oh, it’s just awful. I feel this sharp, sudden panic, almost like a physical jolt in my chest. It’s this overwhelming sense that I’ve completely lost control of the entire system. 

And when that happens, when I see that number go up even a tiny fraction, I just know that I have to correct it immediately. The whole next day has to be adjusted to compensate for that error. I have to recalibrate everything, cut back even further, just to get things back to baseline, back to where they are supposed to be. Because if I don't correct it right away, who knows where it stops? It’s just... it’s a very intense feeling of needing to fix the mistake so things don't spiral out of order. So, yes, I do get upset when the plan changes, mostly because of the consequences on the scale the next day.
Do you have any other daily routines or activities that you feel compelled to perform in a very specific way?

Well, no, not really. I mean, not in the way you're probably thinking. I don't have, you know, rituals where I have to tap a doorframe three times or wash my hands a certain number of minutes. I don't do anything like that. But I do... well, I suppose I do have my ways of doing things, but it's just about efficiency, really. Like with my work, obviously, everything has to be documented in a very specific format, but that's just professional standards. And at home, well, I like my desk arranged just so, because if I'm looking for a specific reference manual or a particular file, I don't want to waste five minutes hunting for it. Time is a resource, after all, and wasting it is just poor management. 

And I guess I do have a very specific morning routine, but again, it's just logical. I wake up at exactly 5:30, I have my coffee—black, of course, because anything else is just unnecessary variables—and then I check my emails before I even look at the news, because the news is just noise, whereas my emails are actionable data. And then, of course, there's the weighing, which we talked about, but that's just part of the data collection for the day. 

But as for feeling "compelled" to do things in a specific way... I don't know if "compelled" is the right word. It's more that I've found the optimal way to do them, so why would I do them any other way? It would be like knowing the fastest route to work and deliberately taking the one with all the traffic lights. It just wouldn't make sense. So, no, I wouldn't say I have any strange compulsions or anything, just a strong preference for keeping my environment and my schedule running as smoothly and predictably as possible. It just keeps the noise down, you know? It keeps everything running the way it should.
Do you feel a strong need for things in your life to be symmetrical or exactly arranged?

Well, symmetry... no, not for the sake of symmetry itself. I mean, I don't look at a room and think, "Oh, that lamp needs to be exactly centered on that table or I can't function." It's not an aesthetic thing, and it's certainly not some irrational need for things to mirror each other. 

But arrangement? Yes, absolutely, things need to be arranged, but again, it all comes back to utility and function. Take my kitchen, for example. I have everything arranged in a very specific order—the measuring cups are exactly where my hand naturally reaches when I open the drawer, the scale is always on the left side of the counter because I'm right-handed and it makes the workflow smoother. The pantry is organized by category and then by expiration date, front to back. But that's not about symmetry. It's about not wasting time rummaging around for a specific brand of broth when I need to make dinner. 

It's the same with my closet. I don't color-code my clothes because it looks pretty; I do it because it reduces decision fatigue in the morning. If I know all the black trousers are in one section, I don't have to spend five minutes trying to distinguish navy from black in the dim light of 5:30 AM. It's just practical. 

I suppose some people might look at my workspace or my home and think it looks a bit... rigid. My sister, for instance, came over last Thanksgiving and made some comment about how my bookshelf looked like a library archive because I have all my reference materials sorted by subject and then alphabetically by author. But honestly, how else are you supposed to find anything? If she needs a book, she spends half an hour tearing her house apart. If I need a book, I have it in my hand in ten seconds. 

So, do I need things exactly arranged? Yes, but only because a disorganized environment leads to an inefficient life. It’s not a compulsion, it’s just good management. I just don't understand people who can live in chaos. It just introduces so many unnecessary variables into your day.
Do you think about your weight or body shape when deciding what to eat?

Well, yes, of course I do. It’s... it’s the primary factor in the decision matrix, really. When I look at a meal, or even just a single item of food, I’m not just thinking about the immediate moment of consuming it. I’m calculating the downstream effects on my physical form. 

And I want to be perfectly clear about this—I know I’m an older woman. I’m sixty-three. I am not under some irrational delusion, and I'm certainly not trying to look young or pretend I'm twenty-five again. That would be completely illogical and, frankly, I find it a bit sad when women my age try to chase their youth like that. 

But... well, I still judge how well I’m handling myself, how well I'm managing my life overall, by my physical shape. Specifically, by whether my waist and my hips look contained in my clothes. "Contained" is exactly the right word for it. If I put on my slacks for work—I have a very specific rotation of tailored trousers for the office—and I feel even the slightest bit of tension at the waistband, or if the fabric pulls even a fraction of an inch across the hips, it’s completely unacceptable to me. It means the system is failing. It means I've miscalculated my intake and allowed things to get sloppy. 

So, when I'm deciding what to eat, I am constantly projecting forward to how those clothes are going to fit the next morning. Will they hang properly, or will I feel... uncontained? Because if a person just lets their waistline expand, it broadcasts a total lack of self-management. In my line of work, if you can't even manage your own physical parameters, how on earth can you be trusted to optimize a complex project or analyze a corporate structure? It all connects. 

So, yes, every single thing I consider eating is evaluated against that exact outcome. Will this keep my shape contained, or will it cause expansion? Because physical expansion is just a physical manifestation of losing control. I actually have this one navy pencil skirt from about ten years ago that serves as a sort of ultimate benchmark for this, and if I even suspect a certain food might make that skirt feel snug, well, the decision is made instantly. I simply won't eat it. Why would I risk compromising the entire structure just for a momentary indulgence? It just wouldn't make any sense.
Are you afraid of gaining weight?

Afraid... well, "afraid" is a very emotional word, isn't it? I prefer to think of it in terms of risk management and maintaining optimal parameters. But, I suppose, if we're being completely honest about the actual physiological response I have... yes. Yes, I am. 

Let me explain it to you the way it actually happens, because it's not just some vague, irrational fear of waking up suddenly heavy one day. It's very specific, and it's entirely tied to the metrics. Let's say I have to go out for a meal. A business dinner, perhaps, or a rare social obligation where I can't completely control the inputs. I try to order optimally, of course—maybe a plain piece of fish, steamed vegetables, explicitly asking them to hold the butter. Which they rarely do properly, by the way, because restaurant kitchens are notoriously undisciplined with fats and sodium, which introduces so many unknown variables. 

But let's say I get through it, and I have what most people would consider a perfectly normal dinner. The next morning, when I do my daily weighing—my data collection, as we discussed—if that scale is up even a pound... well, it’s not just a passing annoyance. It’s this... this incredibly sharp panic. It just hits me right in the chest, this cold, hard realization that I’ve lost control. A whole pound, just from one meal where I let the parameters slip! 

And when that happens, the immediate thought, the only acceptable response, really, is that I absolutely need to correct it the next day. I have to recalibrate the entire schedule to fix that error. I'll mentally map out exactly how much I need to restrict my intake over the next twenty-four hours to get that number back to baseline. Because if I don't correct it immediately, if I just let that pound stay there, it means the system is compromised. It means I've failed to manage myself, and that lack of control is just... it's intolerable to me. So, yes, if you want to call that sharp panic "fear," then absolutely, I am terrified of the data trending upward. It means the whole structure is failing.
Do you engage in regular physical activity or exercise as a way to control your weight?

Exercise? Well, no... no, I don't. And I'll tell you exactly why, because it comes down to basic efficiency. If you look at exercise as a mechanism for weight control, the return on investment is frankly terrible. I mean, think about the mathematics of it. You can spend... what, forty-five minutes on a treadmill, sweating and elevating your heart rate, just to burn maybe three hundred calories? That’s the equivalent of a single bakery muffin. It is infinitely more efficient, from a purely operational standpoint, to simply not consume the muffin in the first place. Zero time expended, zero calories to burn off. 

I see women my age—my sister is a prime example of this, actually—going to these water aerobics classes or spending hours speed-walking around the neighborhood with those ridiculous little pink hand weights. And they spend all this time... I mean, you have to factor in driving to the facility, changing clothes, the class itself, showering afterward, driving back... it’s a massive drain on the daily schedule. I actually calculated it once, just looking at the time expenditure versus the caloric deficit, and the math simply does not support it as a viable primary control method. 

So, no, my system is entirely focused on the input side of the equation. Managing the intake is precise. You can measure it exactly with a digital scale. Exercise, on the other hand, introduces far too many variables. It causes muscle inflammation, it alters water retention... all of which actually obscures the data on the scale the next morning. I remember, oh, it must have been about five years ago, I tried incorporating a stationary bike routine because some medical newsletter suggested it for baseline cardiovascular health. And the very next day, my weight was actually up—due to muscle fluid retention, I assume—and it completely skewed my metrics for the entire week. I couldn't isolate whether it was the food or the exercise causing the fluctuation. 

It’s just... it’s sloppy data management, really. If you want to control the physical parameters, you strictly control the input. Relying on exercise to fix a failure in your intake management is just an inefficient workaround for a flawed system. So, no, I don't exercise to control my weight. I just control the weight.
Is your fear of gaining weight more about how it would affect your health or how it would change your appearance?

Well, as I was trying to explain earlier, it’s... it’s really neither of those things in the traditional sense, or rather, it’s a very specific interpretation of appearance. 

If you mean "appearance" in the sense of vanity, then absolutely not. Like I said before, I know I’m an older woman. I’m sixty-three years old, and I am not under some delusion that I'm going to look twenty-five again. I am not trying to look young, or trying to turn heads, or any of that superficial nonsense. I find that kind of vanity incredibly tedious. But at the same time, it’s not really about health either. I mean, medical health is... it's abstract. Doctors talk about blood pressure or cholesterol, but those are invisible metrics. You can't wake up in the morning and visually verify your cholesterol levels. 

So it all comes back to what I was saying about the visual proof of management. I still judge how well I’m handling myself—how effectively I am operating as a person—by whether my waist and my hips look contained in my clothes. That is the ultimate, undeniable metric for me. 

If I look in the mirror and see physical expansion, if I see my hips pushing against the fabric of my slacks, it’s not that I think, "Oh, I look unattractive." It’s that I think, "I look undisciplined." It’s the appearance of a system failure. I see women my age who just let it all go, wearing these awful, shapeless garments with elastic waistbands, and to me, that just broadcasts to the entire world that they've completely given up on managing their own parameters. They've surrendered control. 

So, yes, it is about my appearance, but purely as a data point. The way my waist and hips fit into my tailored trousers tells me everything I need to know about how well I'm functioning that day. If my shape is contained, then I am contained. My life is contained. If it isn't... well, then I'm failing to handle myself properly, and that is just an unacceptable outcome. It really is the only way I can visually verify that I'm still operating at peak efficiency.
Do you believe that gaining weight would have significant negative effects on your physical health?

Negative effects... well, "health" is such a poorly defined metric the way most people use it, isn't it? If you're asking if I think gaining weight would somehow *improve* my health, which is what my primary care physician seems to believe... well, let me tell you about how those conversations go. 

We have this exact same debate every single time I go in for my routine check-ups. She looks at her little charts, and she looks at the standard BMI index—which, by the way, is a wildly outdated statistical model from the nineteenth century that was never actually intended to evaluate individual health—and she tells me that my current weight is "medically unsafe." That's the exact phrase she uses. Medically unsafe. 

But honestly? When my physician talks about my weight being medically unsafe like that, part of me just thinks she’s vastly overstating the situation. I mean, you have to look at the actual functional outputs. I am sixty-three years old, and I am still working full-time as an operations research analyst, which requires a tremendous amount of sustained cognitive focus and complex problem-solving. I am driving myself everywhere, I am running all my own errands, I am managing my entire life, my household, my portfolios, all with absolute precision. 

If my physical system were truly in some sort of critical danger, as she implies, you would logically see a corresponding drop in my operational capacity, wouldn't you? You'd see me failing to complete daily tasks, or needing assistance, or missing deadlines. But none of that is happening. My daily functioning is completely optimal. 

So when she sits there and tells me I need to gain weight to fix my physical health, I just have to look at the empirical evidence of my own life. Why would I introduce a massive, disruptive variable like weight gain—which, as we've already established, represents a total loss of system control—just to satisfy some generalized medical average, when I am clearly managing my own life perfectly well exactly as I am? It just doesn't hold up to basic logical scrutiny. So, no, I don't see how gaining weight would do anything but negatively impact the highly efficient way I am currently operating.
Do you think gaining weight would affect your health more than your appearance?

Well, again, you're asking me to weigh two concepts—health and appearance—that I feel I’ve already established are just proxies for the real issue here. You're looking at the long-term, theoretical outcomes, but the actual, immediate effect of gaining weight isn't about my cardiovascular system or how I look to a passerby. It’s the immediate, localized crisis of the data itself. 

The real impact is psychological, or rather, operational. Let me give you a very practical example of what I mean. Sometimes, out of sheer necessity—perhaps a professional obligation or a family event—I have to deviate from my standard protocol and have a normal dinner, or, heaven forbid, a restaurant meal. Restaurants are an absolute nightmare of uncontrolled variables, by the way. You have absolutely no idea how much oil the chef is using, the sodium content is invariably off the charts, the portion sizes are totally unstandardized... it's a statistical black hole, frankly. I try to avoid them, but occasionally it's unavoidable.

So, I get through the meal, and I try to estimate the intake as best I can. But the next morning, when I step on my digital scale... if the scale is up even a pound after a normal dinner or a restaurant meal, I don't think about my long-term health, and I certainly don't think about vanity. I feel this... this incredibly sharp, almost physical panic. It’s like a blaring red alarm going off in my head. It tells me that I have completely lost control of my parameters. 

That one pound is a glaring error in the ledger. And the moment I see that number, that sharp panic just takes over, because I know I’ve let the variables overwhelm the system and I need to correct it the next day. I have to immediately calculate the necessary deficit, adjust my intake schedule, and implement a strict correction protocol just to get the data back to baseline. 

So you see, asking if weight gain affects my health or my appearance more is really missing the forest for the trees. The weight gain itself is the system failure. The panic is what affects me. That undeniable, immediate panic that I’ve miscalculated and lost control. That’s the real consequence. Not some abstract medical chart or looking nice in a dress. It’s the sheer terror of inefficiency and having to spend the entire next day fixing a completely avoidable error.
Is your need to control your weight more about avoiding the feeling of being out of control or specifically about the number on the scale?

Well, to me, those two things are inextricably linked. You really can't separate the feeling of control from the actual data point that proves it. As an analyst, I look at... well, I look at absolutely everything through the lens of data and metrics. So the specific number on the scale isn't just a random figure, it is the ultimate metric of my daily efficiency. 

Now, I will admit, my weight has drifted down lately. It's drifted down more than my doctor likes, certainly—she makes that abundantly clear every time I see her, going on and on about her outdated charts and averages. But when I look at the chart, when I sit down at my desk and actually review my own trend lines and the daily figures... I just don't see a problem the way she does. In fact, I still find myself thinking that a little lower would be a cleaner, more manageable number. 

You see, a "clean" number is... it's precise. If a number is hovering at an odd fraction, or if it's fluctuating in a messy, unpredictable range, it feels sloppy to me. It feels like the system isn't fully optimized, like there are loose variables I haven't accounted for. But if I can get it just a little lower, to a precise, distinct target that I've calculated... well, then the ledger is balanced. The parameters are set. 

So, yes, the specific number on the scale is incredibly important, because that exact number is the literal, mathematical proof that I am not out of control. It’s the empirical evidence of my discipline. Without that specific, clean number to verify my status every morning, I wouldn't have any reliable way to measure my operational success for the day. It all comes down to the data.
Is your strict control over food intake primarily driven by a fear of weight gain or by a need to feel in control of your life?

Well, "fear" is such an emotional word, isn't it? And as I’ve been trying to explain, I really operate on logic, on structure. So if you're asking about the primary driver behind my intake... it’s absolutely about maintaining an orderly system. It's about control, yes. In fact, that’s exactly the root of the disconnect I'm having with my primary care physician right now. I really only came in for this evaluation because my doctor seems so incredibly concerned that my meal planning has gotten, as she puts it, "too tight." She looks at my daily intake and sees some sort of... I don't know, some crisis, whereas I look at it and just see a highly optimized schedule. 

Because to me, it just feels like basic time and resource management. Take my mornings, for instance. I start my day quite early, I have a tremendous amount of data to process for my portfolios and my work, so keeping breakfast to just a specific, pre-portioned yogurt... well, it’s simply the most efficient choice. It completely removes decision fatigue right out of the gate. You don't have to think about it, you just execute the protocol. 

And then, as the day progresses, if I’m deep into a complex analysis—which I almost always am—skipping lunch if I’m busy is just a natural consequence of sustained focus. I mean, stopping to procure and consume a mid-day meal would completely disrupt my cognitive flow, and for what? It's an unnecessary interruption. 

And then, by the evening, making a very measured dinner... well, that just ensures the whole day stays perfectly orderly. I calculate the ingredients, I know exactly what the inputs are, and it just nicely balances the ledger before I go to sleep. So when my doctor panics about my routine being too strict, she's completely ignoring the functional utility of it all. It’s not about sitting around terrified of a calorie, it’s about ensuring that my entire day remains predictable, structured, and entirely under my own jurisdiction.
Is your strict control over food intake more about avoiding weight gain or about feeling in control of your daily life?

Well, since we are circling back to this distinction between weight and control, I think I need to clarify how those two concepts actually intersect for me in the physical world. Because it *is* about control, as I've said, but that control has to be verifiable. It has to be tangible. 

Look, I am sixty-three years old. I know I’m an older woman, and I am certainly not operating under some illogical delusion that I’m trying to look young. I have zero interest in chasing after my twenties or trying to fit into some frivolous societal beauty standard. That would be a completely inefficient use of my mental energy. 

But... and this is where the physical reality comes into play... I still judge how well I’m handling myself by my clothing. Specifically, by whether my waist and hips look entirely contained in my clothes. 

It’s a structural assessment, really. When I get dressed in the morning—say I'm putting on a tailored pair of slacks for a board meeting, or even just my standard weekend trousers—I need to feel that there is no deviation in how the fabric falls. If I put those pants on and I feel even a millimeter of tension, if I feel like my waist or my hips are pushing against the seams, expanding beyond their allocated space... well, it’s deeply unsettling. It means the physical form is no longer contained within its established parameters. 

So, avoiding the weight gain isn't about vanity, it's about avoiding that exact sensation of physical spillover. If my hips aren't perfectly contained in my clothes, it tells me that my discipline is slipping, that I am not managing my life effectively. It’s a visible, tactile metric of my competence. People always assume women my age who watch their intake are just desperately trying to fight off aging or look like models, which is honestly quite patronizing. For me, it’s strictly about containment. If the physical boundaries are maintained, then I know the internal system is secure.
Is your strict control over food intake something you feel you need to do to feel safe and in control of your life, rather than just to avoid gaining weight?

Well, I suppose... I mean, yes, the control aspect is paramount, as I've been explaining. But to say it's *rather* than avoiding weight gain... I think that's a false dichotomy, really. Because the weight gain itself is the primary indicator of a loss of control. You can't separate the two. 

Let me give you a very specific example of how this plays out, because I think it perfectly illustrates the mechanism at work here. Let's say, theoretically, that I have a normal dinner. Or, even more problematic, I have to attend a dinner at a restaurant for work—which is always a logistical nightmare because you can't verify the exact inputs, the oils they use, the hidden variables in the preparation. But let's say I do that. I go, I eat, I manage the social obligations. 

The next morning, the scale is the final arbiter of that event. And if I step on that scale and it is up... even by just one pound. Just a single, solitary pound. The reaction I have is... well, it's not a calm, logical assessment. I feel this incredibly sharp, immediate panic. It's a very visceral sensation, right in my chest. It's not just "Oh, the data point shifted." It feels like an alarm going off, signaling that the entire system has been breached. That I have fundamentally lost control of my own physical parameters. 

And that panic... it demands an immediate operational response. I can't just log the data and move on. I feel an overwhelming, absolute necessity to correct it that very next day. The ledger has to be balanced immediately. I have to tighten the protocols, reduce the inputs, maybe extend the fasting window... whatever it takes to get that number back to the established baseline. 

So, is it about safety and control? Yes, absolutely. But the fear of the weight gain—that sharp, undeniable panic when the number goes up—that is the exact mechanism that tells me I am *not* safe. The weight gain is the crisis. So I have to prevent it, at all costs, to maintain the integrity of the whole system.
Is your strict control over food intake something that you feel is necessary to maintain a sense of control in other areas of your life?

Well, it’s all an interconnected system, isn't it? If the foundation is secure, the rest of the structure holds. So, yes, maintaining that strict baseline with my intake is absolutely what allows me to function at the capacity that I do in other areas. 

Because of my routines, I am able to maintain an incredibly high level of productivity. I still keep up with all my analysis work—and as I mentioned earlier, that requires a massive amount of cognitive bandwidth, parsing through complex data sets, identifying trends—and I manage all my household logistics, my errands, everything runs perfectly. It runs like clockwork. The control over my intake doesn't hinder my daily responsibilities at all; if anything, it facilitates them by removing unpredictability. 

However... I suppose if you are looking for areas where the protocols have required some, let's call them, structural adjustments... there are certain social variables I’ve had to eliminate. Just because they introduce entirely too much chaos into the system. 

For example, I belong to a book club. I enjoy the reading, and the intellectual discourse during the actual meeting is perfectly fine, quite stimulating actually. But afterward, the group always insists on migrating to some restaurant or local bistro for a meal. And I’ve... well, I've mostly stopped joining my friends for those meals. I just can't do it anymore. Because sitting there, trying to calculate the hidden inputs in a restaurant kitchen, dealing with the social pressure to order a glass of wine or share an appetizer... it completely throws off the plan I rely on. It disrupts the entire ledger for the day, and for what? A few hours of idle chatter that usually devolves into trivialities anyway once the food arrives? 

It just isn't a logical trade-off. So, I excuse myself. My friends have certainly noticed my absence, of course. They always ask why I have to rush home, and I usually just tell them I have more data to run or an early morning, which is true, in a sense. But the underlying reality is that I simply cannot allow a spontaneous, unverified social dinner to compromise the structure I've built. The cost-benefit analysis just doesn't support it. I need that plan to stay intact so the rest of my life stays intact.
Is your need to control your food intake driven more by the desire to feel in control of your life or the fear of gaining weight?

Doctor, I... I must admit I'm a bit perplexed, because I feel as though we are just iterating the exact same query in a loop, and I'm really not sure what other data point you are looking for here. I don't have a different answer to give you. 

As I've been trying to explain, parsing out whether it's the control over my life or the fear of the weight... it's like asking if I'm more concerned about the engine failing or the car crashing. You simply cannot separate the two in the operational model of my day-to-day existence. I don't know how to quantify which one is "more" of a driver because they are entirely symbiotic. 

If the weight goes up—which, yes, is a massive fear, as I described with the scale—then the control is fundamentally lost. If the control is maintained through my protocols, the weight does not go up, and the fear is kept at bay. I don't have a percentage breakdown for you, like sixty percent control and forty percent weight fear. It just doesn't work like that in my mind. 

I have spent my entire career as an analyst looking at how variables interact, looking at cause and effect and systemic stability. And I can tell you that in this particular system, those two variables are perfectly, undeniably correlated. So if you're asking me to pick one over the other, or to find some new distinction between them, I simply can't do it. I don't have a better way to explain it than what I've already laid out regarding my clothing, the morning weigh-ins, and the social dinners. To me, they are exactly one and the same thing.
Is your strict control over food intake primarily driven by a desire to feel in control of your daily routine?

I... well, again, we are circling back to the routine. But yes, if we are focusing specifically on the daily schedule, the orderliness of it is actually the entire reason I am sitting in your office today. I only came in because my primary care doctor seems highly concerned that my meal planning has gotten entirely too tight. He looked at my charts and decided there was some sort of systemic problem.

But to me, from an operational standpoint, it doesn't feel too tight at all. It just feels like a highly efficient system. It feels like keeping breakfast strictly to a simple, verified portion of yogurt, which requires zero prep time, the inputs are completely consistent, and it gets me right to my desk to start my analysis. Then, as the day progresses and I get deep into my data sets, skipping lunch if I am busy is just a logical reallocation of time. Why break my concentration and disrupt a productive workflow for a meal I don't truly require? It just introduces unnecessary downtime.

And then, by the time evening arrives, making a very, very measured dinner ensures that all the variables are accounted for before the day closes. Everything is precise. So, the routine... yes. Doing it this way means the day stays perfectly orderly. My doctor might view that as a rigid restriction, but to me, it is simply standard operating procedure. It keeps the daily schedule functioning exactly as it should, without any chaotic variables getting in the way.
Is your strict control over food intake something that brings you a sense of comfort and security, or is it primarily a means to avoid a specific outcome?

Well, if I'm being perfectly analytical about it, I'd have to say it's... it's really not an either/or scenario, is it? I mean, comfort and security versus avoiding a specific outcome... they are two sides of the exact same coin. 

Think about it like a risk management model. When I am structuring my intake—when I know exactly what is going into my body, down to the gram, down to the exact caloric value—yes, that provides an immense sense of security.
